      <content name="altTitle">Paget's Disease of <span class="qt2">Breast</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt2">Breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer is a cancer</span></span> that starts in <span class="qt2">breast</span> tissue.  It happens when cells in the <span class="qt2">breast</span> change and grow out of control. New cells grow even when you don't need them, and old cells don't die when they should. These extra cells can form a mass called a <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">tumor</span></span>.</p><p>Sometimes the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> does not spread any further. This is called "in situ." If the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> spreads outside the <span class="qt2">breast</span>, the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is called "invasive." It may just spread to nearby tissues and lymph nodes. Or the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> may metastasize (spread to other parts of the body) through the lymph system or the blood.</p><p><span class="qt2">Breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is the second most common type of <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> in women in the United States. Rarely, it can also affect men.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>There are different types of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. The types are based on which <span class="qt2">breast</span> cells turn into <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. The types include:</p><ul><li>Ductal <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">carcinoma</span></span>, which begins in the cells of the ducts. This is the most common type.</li><li>Lobular <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">carcinoma</span></span>, which begins in the lobules. It is more often found in both <span class="qt2">breasts</span> than other types of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Inflammatory <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer, in which cancer</span></span> cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the <span class="qt2">breast. The breast</span> becomes warm, red, and swollen. This is a rare type.</li><li>Paget's disease of the <span class="qt2">breast</span>, which is a <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> involving the skin of the nipple. It usually also affects the darker skin around the nipple. It is also rare.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt2">Breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> happens when there are changes in the genetic material (DNA). Often, the exact cause of these genetic changes is unknown.</p><p>But sometimes these genetic changes are inherited, meaning that you are born with them. <span class="qt2">Breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> that is caused by inherited genetic changes is called hereditary <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>There are also certain genetic changes that can raise your risk of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, including changes in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These two changes also raise your risk of ovarian and other <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancers</span></span>.</p><p>Besides genetics, your lifestyle and the environment can affect your risk of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>The factors that raise your risk of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> include:</p><ul><li>Older age</li><li>History of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> or benign (noncancer) <span class="qt2">breast</span> disease</li><li>Inherited risk of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, including having BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene changes</li><li>Dense <span class="qt2">breast</span> tissue</li><li>A reproductive history that leads to more exposure to the estrogen hormone, including:
	<ul><li>Menstruating at an early age</li><li>Being at an older age when you first gave birth or never having given birth</li><li>Starting menopause at a later age</li></ul>
</li><li>Taking hormone therapy for meopause</li><li>Radiation therapy to the <span class="qt2">breast</span> or chest</li><li>Obesity</li><li>Drinking alcohol</li></ul>What are the signs and symptoms of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>The signs and symptoms of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> include</p><ul><li>A new lump or thickening in or near the <span class="qt2">breast</span> or in the armpit.</li><li>A change in the size or shape of the <span class="qt2">breast</span>.</li><li>A dimple or puckering in the skin of the <span class="qt2">breast</span>. It may look like the skin of an orange.</li><li>A nipple turned inward into the <span class="qt2">breast</span>.</li><li>Nipple discharge other than <span class="qt2">breast</span> milk. The discharge might happen suddenly, be bloody, or happen in only one <span class="qt2">breast</span>.</li><li>Scaly, red, or swollen skin in the nipple area or the <span class="qt2">breast</span>.</li><li>Pain in any area of the <span class="qt2">breast</span>.</li></ul>How is <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to diagnose <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> and figure out which type you have:</p><ul><li>A physical exam, including a clinical <span class="qt2">breast</span> exam (CBE). This involves checking for any lumps or anything else that seems unusual with the <span class="qt2">breasts</span> and armpits.</li><li>A medical history.</li><li>Imaging tests, such as a mammogram, an ultrasound, or an MRI.</li><li><span class="qt2">Breast</span> biopsy.</li><li>Blood chemistry tests, which measure different substances in the blood, including electrolytes, fats, proteins, glucose (sugar), and enzymes. Some of the specific blood chemistry tests include a basic metabolic panel (BMP), a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and an electrolyte panel.</li></ul><p>If these tests show that you have <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>, you will have tests that study the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells. These tests help your provider decide which treatment would be best for you. The tests may include:</p><ul><li>Genetic tests for genetic changes such in the BRCA and TP53 genes.</li><li>HER2 test. HER2 is a protein involved with cell growth. It is on the outside of all <span class="qt2">breast</span> cells. If your <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells have more HER2 than normal, they can grow more quickly and spread to other parts of the body.</li><li>An estrogen and progesterone receptor test. This test measures the amount of estrogen and progesterone (hormones) receptors in <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> tissue. If there are more receptors than normal, the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> is called estrogen and/or progesterone receptor positive. This type of <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> may grow more quickly.</li></ul><p>Another step is staging the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>. Staging involves doing tests to find out whether the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> has spread within the <span class="qt2">breast</span> or to other parts of the body. The tests may include other diagnostic imaging tests and a sentinel lymph node biopsy. This biopsy is done to see whether the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> has spread to the lymph nodes.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatments for <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> include:</p><ul><li>Surgery such as 
	<ul><li>A <span class="qt2">mastectomy</span>, which removes the whole <span class="qt2">breast</span></li><li>A lumpectomy to remove the <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> and some normal tissue around it, but not the <span class="qt2">breast</span> itself</li></ul>
</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Hormone therapy, which blocks <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells from getting the hormones they need to grow</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells</li><li>Immunotherapy</li></ul>Can <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>You may be able to help prevent <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> by making healthy lifestyle changes such as:</p><ul><li>Staying at a healthy weight</li><li>Limiting alcohol use</li><li>Getting enough exercise</li><li>Limiting your exposure to estrogen by 
	<ul><li>Breastfeeding your babies if you can</li><li>Limiting hormone therapy</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>If you are at high risk, your provider may suggest that you take certain medicines to lower the risk. Some women at very high risk may decide to get a <span class="qt2">mastectomy</span> (of their healthy <span class="qt2">breasts</span>) to prevent <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>It's also important to get regular mammograms. They may be able to identify <span class="qt2">breast</span> <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">cancer</span></span> in the early stages, when it is easier to treat.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt3"><span class="qt4">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>
